en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on False Speech, Section 7: The Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was visiting families in Sāvatthī and frequented many households.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Udāyī dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached a certain family.
At that time, the mistress of the house was sitting at the door of the residence, and the daughter-in-law was sitting at the door of the dwelling.
Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the mistress of the house; having approached her, he taught the Dhamma into her ear.
Then it occurred to the daughter-in-law:
"Is this ascetic the husband's lover, or is he merely flattering her?"
Then the Venerable Udāyī, having taught the Dhamma to the housewife in her ear, approached the daughter-in-law; having approached, he taught the Dhamma to the daughter-in-law in her ear.
Then it occurred to the housewife:
"Is this ascetic the lover of my daughter-in-law, or is he merely making advances?"
Then the Venerable Udāyī, having taught the Dhamma to his daughter-in-law in her ear, departed.
Then the mistress of the house said this to her daughter-in-law:
"Hey, girl, what did that ascetic say to you?"
“Venerable lady, teach me the Dhamma.
“But what did you say to the Venerable Lady?
“She taught the Dhamma to me as well.”
They complained, grumbled, and protested:
“How can the venerable Udāyī teach the Dhamma right into the ear?
Should not the Dhamma be taught with open and clear speech?”
The bhikkhus heard those women criticizing, grumbling, and complaining.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
"How can the venerable Udāyī teach the Dhamma to women?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, Udāyī, that you taught the Dhamma to women?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, teach the Dhamma to a woman?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever monk should teach the Dhamma to a woman, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, laywomen, upon seeing the monks, said this:
"Please, venerable sirs, teach the Dhamma.
"Sister, it is not permissible to teach the Dhamma to women."
“Come now, sisters, teach the Dhamma with five or six words; it is possible to understand the Dhamma even by that much.
“Sister, it is not permitted for women to teach the Dhamma.
Being anxious, they did not teach it.
The female lay followers complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can it be, venerable sirs, that when we are requesting them, they will not teach us the Dhamma?
The monks heard those female lay followers complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to teach the Dhamma to women in five or six sentences.”
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whichever monk should teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, thinking,

“It has been permitted by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma to women with five or six words,” would have an unintelligent man sit down beside them and then teach the Dhamma to women with more than five or six words.
Those monks who were of few desires … [and so on] … complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks, having had an unintelligent man sit down beside them, teach the Dhamma to a woman in more than five or six sentences?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you, having had an unintelligent man sit down beside you, taught the Dhamma to a woman in more than five or six sentences?”

“It is true, Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them: “… How can you, foolish men, having had an ignorant man sit down, teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six sentences? This will not lead to the welfare and happiness of the many, nor to compassion for the world, nor to the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. [The Buddha spoke in many ways in dispraise of being difficult to support, difficult to maintain, and of corrupt livelihoods, and he praised being easy to support, easy to maintain, and pure livelihood. Having rebuked them, the Blessed One gave a teaching on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, one who is ignorant should not be made to sit down so that the Dhamma may be taught to a woman with more than five or six sentences. Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the training rule: “If a bhikkhu, having had an ignorant man sit down, teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six sentences, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the training rule: “If a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six sentences, even if he has not had an ignorant man sit down, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. [The Blessed One then laid down the training rule: “If a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six sentences, whether he has had an ignorant man sit down or not, he commits an offense of wrong-doing. “Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘Whatever monk should teach the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words, except in the presence of a discerning man, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever," means whoever such as [this]... "a monk" means: [as previously defined].
... [as before] ... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
A woman (mātugāma) means a human female;

not a female spirit (yakkhī), not a female ghost (petī), not a female animal; she must be intelligent and capable of discerning what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken, and what is grave and what is trivial.
"More than five or six words" means more than five or six words.
"Dhamma" means:
[The discourse] spoken by the Buddha, spoken by disciples, spoken by seers, spoken by deities, connected with the meaning, and connected with the Dhamma.
If one teaches it by means of the word "should teach," there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every single word.
If she teaches by syllable, for each syllable there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Except with a man who understands" means excluding one who is a man capable of understanding.
A "wise person" is defined as a male human being capable of discerning well-spoken and ill-spoken words, as well as what is indecent and what is not.
If, perceiving a woman to be a woman, one teaches the Dhamma to her by means of more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a wise man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one teaches the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words while in doubt, except when a man of understanding is present, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one teaches the Dhamma to a woman perceiving her as not a woman, with more than five or six words, except when a man of understanding is present, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

If one teaches the Dhamma with more than five or six words to a female *yakkha*, a female *peta*, a *paṇḍaka*, or a female animal in human form, except when a man of understanding is present, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If it is not a woman and he perceives her as a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a woman and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a woman and he does not perceive her as a woman, there is no offense.
There is no offense if she teaches the Dhamma with five or six words to a conscious male person.
He teaches the Dhamma with fewer than five or six words;
he teaches after rising and sitting down again;
he teaches while a woman rises and sits down again.
He teaches another woman,
asks her questions,
and when asked a question, he explains it to her.
If a woman hears one speaking for the sake of something else;
if he is insane;
if he is a first-time offender.
The seventh training rule concerning the teaching of the Dhamma is finished.
